questions.q: Is Cascade Health Analytics, used in this lesson's case study, a real company?
options: No — it's a fictional, illustrative scenario, explicitly not based on a real breach or organization
Yes, it's a real healthcare analytics company whose breach was publicly reported
It's a real company, but the breach details were altered for privacy
The lesson doesn't specify whether it's real or fictional
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly, up front, that Cascade Health Analytics is fictional and illustrative — a realistic composite, not a real incident.

questions.q: What was the root Chapter 1 (RBAC) gap in the case study?
options: The contractor's role was never made time-bound or reviewed as part of an offboarding process
The contractor was never granted any role at all
Too many roles existed in the account
The role hierarchy had too many levels of nesting
questions.explain: The access persisted because nobody owned the step of revoking the grant when the contractor's engagement ended — a review-cadence gap, not an RBAC-design gap.

questions.q: What would a Chapter 2 masking policy have changed about the contractor's lingering access?
options: Even with the stale grant still in place, the contractor would have seen masked values instead of real patient data
It would have automatically revoked the contractor's role after 90 days
It would have prevented the contractor from ever being granted the role
Masking policies have no effect on who can run a SELECT statement
questions.explain: Masking is a second layer of defense: it doesn't fix a stale RBAC grant, but it limits what that stale access can actually expose.

questions.q: Which single query, run as a routine offboarding step, does this lesson say would have caught the gap in minutes?
options: A GRANTS_TO_USERS query filtered to the departed contractor's grantee_name
A query against WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
A query against SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.SESSIONS only
There was no query that could have caught this before the acquisition audit
questions.explain: The Lesson 17-style GRANTS_TO_USERS query, filtered to the contractor's role and deleted_on IS NULL, would have shown the stale active grant immediately.

questions.q: What does this lesson's closing advice say about how governance gaps like this one typically happen?
options: Rarely one dramatic failure — usually several small omissions (no review cadence, no tags, no scheduled monitoring) compounding quietly
Always the result of a single malicious insider
Always caused by a Snowflake platform outage
Only possible on Standard Edition accounts
questions.explain: The case study's point is that each individual gap (RBAC, masking, tags, monitoring, sharing) is small and plausible on its own — it's the combination, unmonitored, that becomes a real exposure.
